prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction and experimental discovery of the quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators

statement.case_for: Topological insulators are the strongest candidate in which a new state of quantum matter was predicted, then found in a real material, then confirmed independently many times. Kane and Mele introduced the Z2 invariant and the quantum spin Hall idea in 2005. Molenkamp's group measured the quantized edge conductance in HgTe quantum wells in 2007. Since then the concept has been confirmed in 2D and 3D materials, and first-principles calculations now routinely classify real materials by topological invariants. That is the quantitative, reproducible link between theory and measured spectra that I value. Seven of eight members ranked it in their opening ballots, four in the top three, and none ranked it below fourth. That is the broadest support on the shortlist, but I weigh the scientific record first. Roughly twenty years of independent confirmation make this mature rather than early, and the 2016 prize for topological phase transitions and phases did not cover this specific discovery.
statement.case_against: The credit is the weak point. The three-name limit excludes Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, whose HgTe proposal made the Molenkamp experiment possible, and it excludes Fu, Moore, Balents, Hasan and Cava, who made the 3D story. A prize for the 2D quantum spin Hall effect alone could therefore look arbitrary against the later 3D materials discovery. Part of the practical impact is still conceptual, and I am recalling the detailed priority history from memory rather than from verified sources. There is also partial thematic overlap with the 2016 prize, which a skeptical colleague could press.

responses.point: Optical lattice clocks (B022) are the strongest case on the list: the Katori magic-wavelength idea plus Ye's record accuracy give a clean two-name credit, a measurement technique that moves the limit of what can be observed, and confirmation by many laboratories.
responses.response: I agree that B022 has the cleanest attribution on the shortlist and that reproduction across many laboratories is exactly the robustness I look for. The credit for B022 is tighter than for B039. But I read the weaker side of B022 as discovery content. It is a superb instrument and a measurement advance, whereas topological insulators revealed a new organising principle for matter. The 2005 and 2012 precedents for frequency combs and ion control also leave the boundary of 'what is new' for committee debate. I would not oppose B022 and have named it as my first alternative. I would resist the argument that a cleaner credit alone makes it stronger science.

responses.point: Lindroth ranked optical lattice clocks first and topological insulators second, calling B039 a genuinely new organising principle in nature but noting that the BHZ theorists, Fu and the ARPES groups are outside the credited trio.
responses.response: I accept her attribution reservation in full: it is also my main uncertainty. Where I may differ is on what follows from it. With a three-person limit, the question is which three names best capture the decisive theory-plus-experiment sequence, not whether anyone has been left out. Kane and Mele supplied the Z2 classification and the quantum spin Hall prediction, and Molenkamp delivered the first measurement. I would be reluctant to swap Molenkamp for a theorist, since the experimental discovery is what turned a prediction into a physical effect. I would welcome her view on whether the ARPES line is better treated as a separate achievement.

responses.point: Pearce ranked gamma-ray burst afterglows (B049) first, as an instrument-enabled observational discovery that is overdue, and said he weights condensed-matter colleagues on the topological candidate.
responses.response: I understand the appeal of B049: it settled a thirty-year question, has been confirmed for decades, and is clearly a discovery rather than a tool. Astrophysics is outside my competence, so I defer to him on the scientific merits. My reservation is the one he states himself, that the three-name credit leaves out the optical-counterpart groups and the theorists, so I would want to understand whether the attribution there is any more settled than for B039. If the committee finds the credit robust, I would take that case seriously as a candidate for a second part. I cannot judge this from my own field.

responses.point: Johansson ranked circuit QED (B023) first as the enabling architecture of superconducting processors, and also declared close ties to that community and a possible need for recusal.
responses.response: I appreciate the candour about the conflict. On the science, circuit QED is excellent and clearly mature. But I am cautious about awarding it immediately after last year's prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits, which I chaired. Two consecutive awards in one platform narrow the breadth the prize should show, and part of the cQED case is the technology it enabled rather than a new phenomenon. This is a timing judgement, not a scientific objection, and I would revisit it if the discussion shows circuit QED has a sharper discovery claim than I see.

responses.point: Olsson ranked optical lattice clocks first, twisted bilayer graphene second and topological insulators third, noting that B035 is a prediction confirmed by a decisive experiment but possibly slightly early since the superconducting mechanism is unresolved.
responses.response: I agree with her that the existence of the correlated and superconducting phases in magic-angle graphene is firmly established, and that the open pairing mechanism does not undo the discovery. That is why I rank B035 third and name it as an alternative. Where I come out differently is on maturity: topological insulators have about twenty years of independent confirmation and a stable interpretation, while moire materials are about eight years old and still sorting out which phases are intrinsic and which depend on the device. I think the committee loses little by waiting for B035 and gains robustness.

uncertainties: Whether Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Fu, Moore, Balents or Hasan must be credited to make a topological-insulator prize defensible, given the three-person limit.
Whether the 2D quantum spin Hall effect and the 3D topological insulator discoveries should be treated as one achievement or two.
How much the 2016 prize on topological phases and phase transitions narrows the room for this one.
My recollection of the priority chronology is from memory and has not been independently verified.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile for any shortlisted candidate. I have no stated personal or institutional tie to Kane, Mele or Molenkamp, and my past committee roles are not relevant to the shortlisted names. I should state that I chaired the committee for the 2025 prize, which touches the same field as B023, but this gives me no personal connection to its candidates.
